L.meaning: L is a field under the operations induced from K
L.source_sentence:
Commentary
|-
| 1 || Let SYM(L) be the center of SYM(K), i.e., the subset of SYM(K) comprising those elements that commute multiplicatively with every element of SYM(K). || || || || || 
|-
| 2 || SYM(L) is a field under the operations induced from SYM(K), and the multiplicative group SYM(L^*) of nonzero elements of SYM(L) is the center of SYM(K^*). || || SYM(K) is a division ring || || <toggledisplay>SYM(L) is an additive subgroup of SYM(K) because of the distributivity laws relating addition and multiplication.

\\alpha.source_sentence: If SYM(d = \alpha r_i + \beta) where SYM(\alpha) is the quotient and SYM(\beta) is the remainder, we get SYM(q^{\alpha r_i + \beta} \equiv 1 \pmod{q^{r_i} - 1}).

\\beta.source_sentence: If SYM(d = \alpha r_i + \beta) where SYM(\alpha) is the quotient and SYM(\beta) is the remainder, we get SYM(q^{\alpha r_i + \beta} \equiv 1 \pmod{q^{r_i} - 1}).

r_i.source_sentence: Then, as an integer, SYM(A) divides SYM(q^d - 1) as well as each of the quotient SYM((q^d - 1)/(q^{r_i} - 1)) appearing in step (7). || || || Steps (7), (8) || <toggledisplay>Since each SYM(r_i) is a proper divisor of <matH>d</math>, the polynomial SYM(\Phi_d(x)), as a polynomial, divides SYM(x^d - 1) and each of the quotients SYM((x^d - 1)/(x^{r_i} - 1)) -- we can see this by considering the roots of these polynomials.

q.source_sentence: Since SYM(q) is a positive integer, the only root of unity that's a positive real multiple of it is SYM(1), so equality holds only if SYM(\zeta = 1), which in turn could happen only if SYM(d = 1).
